items.concept: Doctors told parents to put babies to sleep on their stomachs for 40 years. Then in 1992, the AAP reversed the advice: back is best. The Back to Sleep campaign cut SIDS deaths by 50% in just 5 years. Tens of thousands of babies survived who wouldn't have — because of one sentence of changed medical guidance.

scene-3.text: Tens of thousands of babies who would have died survived — because of one updated sentence in medical guidelines. The simplest intervention in modern pediatrics.

items.hook_text: FIRST PRICE YOU SEE LOCKS YOU
items.concept: The first price you see permanently anchors your expectations — retailers know this. They place $500 sunglasses at store entrances so $150 ones feel like a bargain. Luxury car showrooms display the $120K model first. The anchor is set in milliseconds and your brain never fully resets. It's called anchoring bias and every retailer exploits it.

scene-1.text: The first price you see permanently anchors your expectations. Retailers know this. You don't.

scene-2.text: They place $500 sunglasses near entrances so $150 ones feel like a steal. Luxury car showrooms open with the $120,000 model. That anchor is set in milliseconds — and your brain never fully resets it. It's called anchoring bias.

scene-3.text: Every major retailer engineers their floor plan around this. Next time you feel like you're getting a deal — ask what they showed you first.

items.concept: Lottery winners' neighbors go bankrupt at measurably higher rates than matched control groups. The effect is so documented economists have a name for it: 'expenditure cascades.' When you see visible wealth next door — new car, new boat, renovation — your brain interprets normal as inadequate. The spending is contagious and it doesn't even require friendship.

scene-1.text: When your neighbor wins the lottery, your bankruptcy risk goes up. This is documented. It has a name.
scene-1.direction: bold controversy hook — unexpected, slightly alarming

scene-2.text: Economists call it expenditure cascades. When visible wealth appears next door — new car, new boat, renovation — your brain recalibrates what's normal. Your spending goes up to match what you can see. The effect is contagious without even a conversation.
scene-2.direction: informative, building — explain the mechanism clearly

scene-3.text: Researchers tracked Canadian lottery winners and their immediate neighbors. The closer you lived and the bigger the win, the higher your odds of financial distress. Comparison isn't just emotional — it's economic.

items.concept: Stable Diffusion and DALL-E don't 'draw' images — they reverse noise. They were trained on billions of image/text pairs and learned to identify what structured visual information looks like when hidden inside random static. To generate an image, they start with pure noise and mathematically subtract the randomness until a coherent picture emerges. It's a denoise engine, not an artist.

scene-1.text: AI image generators don't draw. They reverse noise. That distinction changes everything about how they work.
scene-1.direction: bold, counter-intuitive hook — land the surprise immediately

scene-2.text: Stable Diffusion was trained on billions of image-text pairs. It learned to recognize what structured information looks like hidden inside random static. To create an image, it starts with pure noise — and mathematically removes the randomness until something coherent appears.
scene-2.direction: informative, slightly technical but accessible — build the mental model

scene-3.text: It's not an artist. It's a denoising engine. The creativity is in the training data and the prompt. The model's job is just subtraction — removing everything that isn't the picture.

captions.youtube: AI image generators don't 'draw' — they reverse random noise into pictures. Here's how it actually works. #aifacts #stablediffusion #aiart #machinelearning
captions.instagram:

It's not an artist. It's a denoising engine.

items.concept: Google's DeepDream runs a neural network backwards — with no input, just amplifying its own internal activations in a feedback loop. The result is psychedelic images that reveal exactly what patterns the AI learned to recognize. Dog faces in clouds. Eyes in leaves. Pagodas in mountains. The hallucinogenic visuals aren't art — they're a direct window into what the network's neurons respond to.

scene-1.text: When Google ran their AI backwards — no input, just its own brain amplifying itself — this is what came out.

scene-2.text: It's called DeepDream. The neural network runs in reverse, amplifying whatever patterns its neurons already respond to. Dog faces emerge from clouds. Eyes appear in leaves. Towers grow from mountains. The psychedelic images aren't art — they're the neural network's internal vocabulary made visible.
scene-2.direction: informative, slightly trippy tone — match the content

scene-3.text: Every AI image recognition system has this hidden visual language. DeepDream just made it audible. When your phone recognizes your face, it's running the same underlying patterns — just not in reverse.
